text: My name's Jake, and I lead our Labs team here at LangChain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Whether you're building a coding agent, a support agent, a research agent, most teams arrive at the general same instinct that it should get better from one run to the next.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let me give you an example to hold on to for the rest of this talk today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Recently, the Labs team at LangChain have been working with a company in the financial services sector who's building a spending, budgeting, and non-investment advice agent.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you can imagine in some contexts, and actually in some contexts that we experienced, its tone would slip.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so it would move from being advisory and helpful to actually pointed and directed, saying things like,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Users in your similar situation would generally set a spending cap, and it would actually say, oh, well, actually, it looks like you need to cancel some subscriptions and move some money into savings.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The company that we're working with thought that this is a violation of tone, and there were similar instances of this, too.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You have to have someone understand the traces and understand where its tone slipped, make those changes to the context that it needs to reference when it's giving its tone,

text: Obviously, that doesn't scale or rather is challenging to scale.

text: And so the system should be or the system around the agent should be a place where it can continuously learn and benefit from its interactions and its experiences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's the version of memory that I want to talk about today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Together, I want to start with the tension that I think a lot of teams have run into.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think all of us here today, the reason why we're at this conference is we're curious, we're building agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think we've gotten very good at observing them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But observing them and then turning those observations and those agent experiences into lessons for future runs are obviously very different things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that's where memory comes into play.

text: Agents are producing more signal and more traces than ever before.

text: And this is going to be something that will obviously increase as more agents are built.

text: That's fantastic for us because every run produces a trace, and that trace is stored somewhere.

text: That's incredibly useful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It means that we can understand the tools that were called, the reasoning that the agent made as it was on its way to making its decision, the artifacts that it referenced.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Observability is obviously a critical foundation for building very reliable agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But I think the challenge really is after the trace is stored or after the log or after the transcript of what the agent did is stored.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If the future context that that agent references never changes, then a misguided skill or instruction will mean that the agent, the mistake that the agent makes today will still persist in future runs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The goal or the system that we want to work towards is where a trace stops just being a log and becomes a source of signal.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents that are observable tell you what happened.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents that are adaptive are able to change and guide themselves on the following runs.

text: So I've mentioned memory.

text: I think it'll really help to sort of define what I mean when I say memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's the durable context that an agent references that will guide future runs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A trace, a transcript, or a log is evidence of what happened.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It only becomes memory when that lesson is converted into durable context that the agent can reference on future runs.

text: Now you'll see six things on this slide behind me, facts, preferences, patterns, previous examples, skills, and instructions.

text: I think that it's helpful to group them into three distinct buckets, a taxonomy that we borrow from cognitive science, and actually it applies a lot when we're talking about agents that are language-based.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, there's what the agent knows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is often referred to as semantic memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This includes things like the facts and the preferences that guide the way that it responds.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then there's what the agent has experienced.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is the episodic memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is the learned patterns that it's seen, past interactions and examples.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And finally, there's how the agent should behave.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is also known as procedural memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's the instructions, the skills that you're all probably very familiar with, and the rules that guide how it should behave.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Procedural memory is where actually most of the visible gains come from.

text: So in that financial assistant that I, the example that I gave at the beginning, tone changes that we wanted to promote to the agent and make it follow came in the form of updating its procedural memory.

text: We were giving it a rule to follow as it engages with its users.

text: That's the procedural memory that guides our agent.

text: Another distinction that I want to make, and I think this is very important when thinking about the general agent memory paradigm, is the separation between working memory or short-term memory and long-term memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Working memory is what the agent is referencing in its current run.

text: So these might be things like intermediate scratch pads.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It might be tool results.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It might be the files retrieved as part of its operation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everything that it needs to do to perform its current job,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Long-term memory is what exists typically in some data structure or some store somewhere else that has instructions and skills and things that it needs to reference as part of future turns and continuous behavior.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Different agent harnesses will leverage and inject long-term memory in different ways, whether you're building your own SDK or using a variety of different popular agent frameworks.

text: Some inject it directly into the prompt.

text: Some will use tools to retrieve that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some will pull it directly from the store.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some load it through files, or some change the runtime state.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The implementation can vary, but the distinction is really important.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some of the memory or some of the context that an agent references is temporary, while some of it is durable and long term and is useful to guide future runs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I think that distinction is really important when we think about traces and logs and artifacts that the agent produces as it runs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A trace isn't just a record of the final output.

text: It's a record of how our working memory changed over the course of the run.

text: Some part of that should stay as history.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some part of that should become durable long-term context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so that's what lends itself to this really helpful mental model that I have, or that I and the team at LangChain and generally I think is a very useful way to sort of think about the relationship between working or short-term memory and long-term memory.

text: It's a read-write cycle.

text: And so you might have heard of sleep time compute or dreaming.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's the sleep time compute.

text: That's that phase moving from long-term memory into short-term memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then when the agent runs, it produces a trace.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As I mentioned, most evidence should stay as history.

text: If we turned everything that was, if we turned all of that evidence into long-term memory, then it would make the agent struggle, and it would make it harder to reason over future tasks.

text: And so what I think is really interesting is the filter step.
